q: A label may add Les Bessards, Le Meal or L'Hermite beneath the appellation name. What are those?
exp: The hill is a patchwork of granite, loess and stony terraces, and the parcels taste different enough to name. Most estates still blend across several of them for their principal wine.

q: Eleven communes wrapping around that hill carry far more vines than the hill itself. Which appellation covers them?
exp: It is the workhorse of the north and the usual first taste of northern Syrah, since the volume keeps the price within reach. Its southern sector is flat glacial gravel, while the northern communes are granite slopes much like Hermitage itself.

q: Two bottles of that same appellation can taste unrelated, the first lean and firm, the second soft and forward. What best explains it?
opts: It permits both Syrah and Mourvedre for red
One is a village wine and the other a cru
One is white and the other red
It takes in both granite slopes and a stony plain
exp: The northern sector around Gervans and Larnage is hillside granite; the southern sector is flat alluvial ground. Knowing which half a wine comes from tells you more than the vintage does.

q: Blending a little Marsanne or Roussanne into the red is legal on the hill of Tain. Up to what proportion?
exp: Very few producers use it now, though the tradition is old and was once thought to soften the tannin. The allowance is a permission rather than an instruction.

q: A ribbon of vineyard runs some fifty kilometres along the right bank, from Chavanay in the north to Guilherand in the south. Which appellation?
exp: Stretching an appellation that far means the quality is uneven, since the granite heart of it around Tournon and Mauves sits alongside far flatter land. Producer matters more here than in any other northern cru.

q: Steep granite terraces in a sheltered amphitheatre ripen Syrah earlier than anywhere else in the north, and no white grape may enter the wine at all. Which appellation?
exp: The name is said to come from a Celtic term for burnt earth. Hills behind the village block the north wind, so it ripens ahead of its neighbours and gives the darkest, most tannic of the northern reds.

q: Still whites and a sparkling wine, both from Marsanne and Roussanne, with no red permitted whatever. Which appellation faces Valence across the river?
exp: The southernmost appellation of the north and the least seen abroad. Its sparkling wine was fashionable in the nineteenth century and has been quietly recovering ground since.

q: Of the two whites permitted at Hermitage and Saint-Joseph, one is planted far more widely because it yields reliably and resists disease better. Which?
exp: It gives the weight and the waxy texture; its partner gives perfume and acidity but is a nuisance in the vineyard. Most blends lean heavily on the easier grape.

q: Reds from that long right-bank ribbon may take a small share of white grapes, less than Hermitage allows. What is the limit?
exp: The rule mirrors Hermitage at a lower level, and as there it is used sparingly. Cornas alone among the northern reds permits nothing at all.

q: Bubbles in the sparkling wine of Saint-Peray come from a second fermentation carried out where?
opts: In a sealed tank under pressure
By injecting carbon dioxide before bottling
In the bottle, as in Champagne
In a single fermentation halted by cold
exp: The traditional method, so the wine is bottle-fermented and riddled, but built from Marsanne and Roussanne rather than Chardonnay. The result is broader and less taut than a sparkling wine from a cooler region.

q: Fermenting Syrah with a proportion of its stems left in the vat is common practice in the north. What does whole-bunch inclusion usually contribute?
opts: Aromatic lift and a firmer tannic frame
Extra sweetness from sugar in the stems
exp: Green stems can add a bitter, stalky note, so the decision turns on how ripe the wood is. Stems also absorb some colour, so the wine often ends up a shade lighter rather than darker.

q: Peppery aroma in cool-vintage Syrah has been traced to one aroma compound. Which?
exp: It also occurs in black pepper itself, which is why the descriptor is so exact. Warm sites and hot years suppress it, so the pepper fades as you move south down the valley.

q: Weight, almond and a waxy texture come from one of the two northern whites; perfume, pear and firmer acidity from the other, which is fickle in the vineyard. Which is the fickle one?
exp: It ripens late, rots easily and oxidises quickly, so growers plant it for what it brings to a blend rather than for an easy life. Its name refers to the russet colour of the ripe skin.

q: The black grape behind every northern Rhone red is called something else in Australia. Which name?
exp: The same grape, and the name is now a rough style signal: the French spelling tends to promise pepper and restraint, the Australian one ripeness and sweet fruit.

q: Traditional northern cellars matured Syrah in large old casks rather than in new barriques. What is such a cask called?
exp: Big and old means slow, gentle oxygen exchange and almost no oak flavour. Many estates that experimented with new barrels have drifted back toward larger wood.

q: Plantings of one northern white had fallen to a few hectares by the late 1960s before a worldwide revival. Which grape?
exp: It came within a generation of disappearing, then became fashionable and was planted from California to Australia. Condrieu remains the reference point for what it can do.
